RR Auction's auction of Steve Jobs' 1968 science fair project has concluded, with the handmade exhibit ultimately selling for $34,375. Here are the details.

“Overall condition is very fine to excellent”

A few days ago, we reported on the auction of an eighth-grade science fair project created by Steve Jobs in 1968.

The project, focused on silicon-controlled rectifiers, included two demonstration circuits and a 10-page report, and online bidding had not yet reached $3,000 at the time.

As one of the lots in the “Steve Jobs and the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction, Part II,” bidding for the item has ended, with a final sale price of $34,375, as first reported by MacRumors.

According to RR Auction, the project “spent decades in the famed ‘Apple garage’ property,” having been kept by Jobs' family. His stepbrother, John Chovanec, said Jobs repeatedly refused to take the project back and ultimately agreed to let Chovanec keep it.

The “Steve Jobs and the Computer Revolution: The Apple 50th Anniversary Auction, Part II” featured nearly 150 Apple and technology-related treasures, including a business card personally signed by Steve Jobs, a batch of electronic components personally owned by Jobs, and a letter in which he politely declined a speaking invitation in 1983, which sold for $156,658, $27,188, and $24,695, respectively.

However, the highest-selling item was a fully functional Apple-1 computer, one of the second batch of 50 produced, which ultimately sold for $499,363.

Do you own any rare Apple memorabilia? Feel free to let us know in the comments section.
